title: ayam atma brahma — a week each
hook: honey: where everything feeds everything, and the great saying lands
carry: ayam atma brahma — a week each
tomorrow: what do a teacher and a student say before a hard lesson?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma through Om: three sounds, and a silence two schools hear in their own ways. Today the Brihadaranyaka reaches the same saying through something you can taste.

Honey in tea for a sore throat, honey on toast, honey stuck to the side of the jar. It's slow and sticky, and it was made by creatures that needed the same flowers everyone else did. The Brihadaranyaka stops, in the middle of its biggest teachings, to talk about exactly that. A long passage, almost a song, about what feeds what. And when it finally lands, it lands on ayam atma brahma.
screen: `HONEY IN THE TEA.` → `WHAT FEEDS WHAT.` → `IT LANDS ON THE SAYING.`

segments.voice: The passage is called the honey teaching, madhu. It goes around the world one thing at a time. This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth. The waters, the same. Fire, wind, the sun, the sky, the moon, lightning, thunder: each one honey for all beings, and all beings honey for it. Nothing here only gives or only takes. Everything feeds, and is fed. And in each one, the text says, there is a shining, deathless person, and the same shining person within the body. That one is the self. Then the close: this self is Brahman, the experiencer of all. So the Mandukya reached the saying through a sound and its silence. The Brihadaranyaka reaches it through a world where everything is food for everything else. Two roads, one line. And with it, a set is complete. Tradition gathers four great sayings, one from the Upanishads of each Veda: prajnanam brahma, from the Aitareya; aham brahmasmi, from the Brihadaranyaka; tat tvam asi, from the Chandogya; and ayam atma brahma, from the Mandukya. Each Vedanta school reads them in its own way, and now all four have had their turn.
screen: `MADHU: THE HONEY TEACHING.` · `EVERYTHING FEEDS, AND IS FED.` · `THE SAME SHINING PERSON WITHIN.` · then, large: `FOUR SAYINGS, ONE FROM EACH VEDA.`

segments.voice: If there's honey near you, or anything sweet, take a little and let it rest on your tongue before you swallow. Trace it back: the flower, the rain, the ground, the hands that carried it to you. If there's nothing to taste, breathe in slowly and notice the air feeding you, and your breath warming it in return.
Ayam atma brahma, the honey way: everything feeds and is fed, and in each, the same shining self. The last day with this saying.
For the road: ayam atma brahma — a week each, honey for all beings, and all beings honey for it. Four sayings, done.

howItsDone: Students of the Brihadaranyaka read the honey teaching (2.5) as one long passage, and teachers often present the four mahavakyas together, one from the Upanishads of each Veda, at the end of studying them.
